ctx.x: Another fellow who became quite friendly with the band was an Egyptian musician who played drum. His name was Pierre Fouad. He had recorded with Django and had quite a solid beat with brushes. He also invited us to dinner at his home and he had a fine collection of records also.

It was there that I heard for the first time Billie Holiday's recording of 'Miss Brown To You' with Teddy Wilson at the box. Fouad also had a photo of Bunny Berigan whom I had heard but never seen. Bunny's recording of 'I Can't Get Started with you' was the greatest he ever did to my estimation. And it is the only record other than some of Louis's that I copied note for note and I still play it the way Bunny did at times just for my own pleasure.

items.q: But the surprise of the night and it was an unexpected one, was that Billie Holliday was at Minton's this night... Eventually someone asked Billie to sing and she did not refuse. I've always dug Lady Day from the first time I heard her, so this pleased me to hear her once again in person.

ctx.x: When Ryan's place closed, Oscar offered to take us up town to Minton's Playhouse. We had no idea of what group was playing there but that didn't matter because Minton's always had good musicians playing there. And one of my old bosses, Teddy Hill was the manager and I'm almost certain that he was at least part owner of the place. I had not seen Teddy since 1946 when we met on a street in Manila in the Philippines and we were happy to see each other again.

But the surprise of the night and it was an unexpected one, was that Billie Holliday was at Minton's this night. Not engaged to sing there but as a client the same as we were. Eventually someone asked Billie to sing and she did not refuse. I've always dug Lady Day from the first time I heard her, so this pleased me to hear her once again in person. And it was a great thrill for Lily because she liked her records very much and now she could see and hear the Lady Day in the flesh.

Oscar would not let me pay for anything and somewhere during the morning, we had picked up Al Hall who was with us at Minton's. We left Teddy Hill about 6 a.m. and Al suggested that we go to his place for breakfast. We also had with us Joan Hill, who had been my common law step-daughter, if some law of that kind exists. Joan didn't get along too well with her mother, Beezie. She was twenty years old, six feet tall and had a baby of six months, Steve. She left us to go and fetch the baby and said she would rejoin…
